items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 172: Duty to promote the success of the company
items.quote: the impact of the company's operations on the community and the environment
items.why: The duty that applies to every director of every company, whatever its size. In promoting the company's success for its members, a director must have regard to six listed matters, including long-term consequences and the impact on the community and the environment. It is a duty to have regard, not a duty to achieve an outcome, and it names no sustainability officer.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 414CB: Contents of non-financial and sustainability information statement
items.locator: s.414CB(A1) and (2A)(a) to (h); notes F4 and F7
items.quote: a description of the company’s governance arrangements in relation to assessing and managing climate-related risks and opportunities
items.why: The binding disclosure rule on governance. Companies in scope must describe, in the strategic report, their governance arrangements for climate-related risks and opportunities, together with risk management, targets and the indicators used. Inserted by S.I. 2022/31. Climate only; wider environmental and social matters are covered by subsection (1) for a narrower group of companies.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 414CA: Non-financial and sustainability information statement
items.quote: if in that year the company’s turnover was more than £500 million
items.why: Who must make the governance disclosure. Traded, banking and insurance companies, companies on the Alternative Investment Market, and companies with turnover of more than £500 million, in each case only if they have more than 500 employees. Small and medium-sized companies are excluded by subsection (3). This is the basis for saying that smaller companies have no such duty.

items.title: UK SRS S2: Climate-related Disclosures
items.locator: Paragraphs 5 and 6 (governance), PDF page 7; paragraph 29(g) (remuneration), PDF page 16
items.quote: how and how often the body(s) or individual(s) is informed about climate-related risks and opportunities
items.why: The fullest statement of what governance of sustainability looks like on paper: name the body or individual responsible for oversight, say how the responsibility appears in terms of reference and role descriptions, how often they are informed, how trade-offs are weighed, how targets are overseen and whether pay is linked. Based on the international standard IFRS S2. Published by government in February 2026; the document does not itself say who must apply it.

items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.locator: Section 1, Principle A and Provision 1, p.6; Section 5, Principle P, p.15
items.quote: ensure that the necessary resources, policies and practices are in place for the company to meet its objectives and measure performance against them
items.why: The board's role stated in terms of long-term sustainable success and contribution to wider society, and remuneration designed to support it. Applies through the FCA's Listing Rules on a comply or explain basis, so it binds listed companies only; for others it is a benchmark. The Code does not name a sustainability owner or use the term ESG.

items.title: Recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures: Final Report
items.publisher: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
items.locator: Section C, 'Governance', recommended disclosures a) and b) with guidance for all sectors, PDF page 27
items.quote: whether the organization has assigned climate-related responsibilities to management-level positions or committees
items.why: The international origin of the board-oversight and management-role questions that UK law and the UK standards now ask. Sets out what a description of board oversight should cover: how often the board is informed, whether climate is considered in strategy and budgets, and how progress against targets is monitored. Voluntary recommendations; the task force has since disbanded and its work passed to the IFRS Foundation, which was not checked in this pass.

items.title: Thematic Review: Climate-related Financial Disclosures by AIM and Large Private Companies
items.locator: Section 1 'Executive summary', key findings (PDF page 4); section 3 'Scope and selection' (PDF page 7); section 7 'Governance arrangements' (PDF page 13)
items.quote: the extent of the integration of the climate governance process with the company’s overall governance process was often unclear
items.why: Source of the quotation and the figure. The regulator read the first mandatory climate disclosures of 20 companies with more than 500 employees. Almost all described governance, but often without showing how a climate committee related to the board; only half gave all the required information on targets and progress. Limits: 20 companies chosen by the regulator, year-ends August to December 2023, climate only.

items.title: PPN 006: Technical standard for completion of Carbon Reduction Plans
items.quote: Your Carbon Reduction Plan must be signed off by a director (or equivalent) or designated member (for LLPs).
items.why: The one place found where a UK rule requires board-level ownership of a sustainability document from a company of any size: a supplier bidding for a central government contract in scope must state that the board has approved its plan, with the date, and name the director who signed it. Applies only to those procurements.

items.title: Voluntary sustainability reporting standard for non-listed SMEs (VSME)
items.locator: Comprehensive Module, disclosure C2, paragraphs 48 and 49, PDF page 12; template at paragraph 213 (source of the quoted words)
items.quote: You may indicate the highest senior level in the undertaking accountable for implementing them [if any]
items.why: Checks the claim in the existing briefing that the European voluntary standard asks who is accountable. It does, but as an option ('may indicate, if any') attached to the description of practices and policies, not as a required governance disclosure. EFRAG's own text; its status in EU law was not checked here. Not UK law.

items.title: ClientEarth v Shell plc and others [2023] EWHC 1897 (Ch)
items.publisher: High Court of Justice, Chancery Division (The National Archives, Find Case Law)
items.quote: it is for directors themselves to determine (acting in good faith) how best to promote the success of a company
items.why: The leading UK decision on directors' duties and climate risk. A shareholder sought permission to sue Shell's directors for their handling of climate risk; the court refused, holding that how the listed matters are weighed is for the directors and that no prima facie case had been shown. It shows the limit of section 172 as a lever: the duty is real, but courts will not second-guess a board's balance. A first-instance permission decision; any later appeal was not checked.
